description: Learning and Exploring our Limits and what we can achieve through a hackathon as a team of diverse knowledges.
summary:
Oxyflame is a mission-aware dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments into honest fire-safety guidance for spacecraft and habitats. Pick a crew environment: ISS, a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover, a Mars habitat, a spacesuit and Oxyflame ranks the relevant NASA investigations, answers plain-language questions with every number tied to its source, and judges whether two experiments can fairly be compared or whether a confounder blocks it. When the data can’t support a claim, it says so, and it names the experiment that would close the gap.
This addresses Flame in Freefall directly: almost all combustion data comes from orbit (~0 g) or Earth (1 g), while the Moon (0.165 g) and Mars (0.38 g) sit in an under-tested middle. By mapping exactly where the evidence ends, never labeling a material “safe” or “unsafe”. Oxyflame helps mission planners base fire-safety decisions on cited evidence instead of guesswork.
details:
Oxyflame turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into a fire-safety decision tool. You pick one of seven crew environments — Earth, ISS, two lunar cases, a pressurized rover, a Mars habitat, or a spacesuit — and it does four things: Atlas ranks NASA’s combustion investigations for that scenario (showing “Cannot assess” instead of a score when oxygen or pressure isn’t documented); Ask answers a plain-language question in six parts (verdict, cited sentences, what differs, limit, next step, scope), with every number checked against the record it cites; the Referee judges whether a difference between two experiments can honestly be pinned on one variable; and Missing experiment names the test that would close the gap. Every value links to its NASA source. Oxyflame never calls a material “safe” or “unsafe”, it shows what the evidence supports and where it ends.

Problem and impact. Almost all NASA combustion data comes from orbit (~0 g) or Earth (1 g); the Moon (0.165 g) and Mars (0.38 g) sit in between with little direct data, and partial gravity isn’t bounded by those two points. Planners need to know where the evidence ends before relying on it. Oxyflame makes that boundary explicit so lunar and Mars fire-safety decisions rest on cited evidence and clearly-marked gaps.

Tools. Python ingest (Playwright PSI scraper, PDF parsing, release pipeline) builds a dataset where every value carries its source, page, and evidence type. A deterministic TypeScript rules engine (Vitest-tested) runs ranking, the Referee, and the planner. The backend is entirely on Cloudflare (Workers, Workers AI/bge-m3 embeddings, Vectorize, KV, Pages — free plan); the frontend is React + Vite + Tailwind as a website and an installable offline mobile PWA, plus a Twilio SMS/WhatsApp webhook. Gemini only proposes wording and is used only if a citation validator confirms every number matches a source; otherwise a template answer shows. Data: NASA PSI and NTRS reports (Saffire I–VI, BASS/BASS-II, FM2 Moon) — 25 investigations indexed, 12 runs, all 12 verified against their NASA source.

Creativity. Oxyflame’s principle is honesty about uncertainty: every run is human-verified against the primary PDF by a second reviewer, the AI can’t cite a number that isn’t sourced, the Referee names the confounder blocking a comparison, and the app points to the next experiment. We weighed scientific integrity, provenance, accessibility (offline + SMS), and cost (zero-billing deployment).
